answer: I'd like to describe a time I helped a new colleague at the education consultancy where I work. A time I clearly remember helping someone was when a younger colleague was struggling badly with a project and close to panicking. It was during our busiest season last year, and he had been asked to prepare several students' university applications with very tight deadlines. He was new and clearly [[overwhelmed]], afraid to admit he was falling behind. I noticed he seemed stressed, so I quietly offered to sit with him after work and go through it together. Over a couple of evenings, we broke the task into manageable steps and slowly untangled the problem. I also showed him the checklist I use for each application and how to deal with the most urgent deadlines first. What I found most [[rewarding]] was watching his confidence gradually return as things started to make sense. He was incredibly grateful, though honestly, helping him did not feel like a chore at all. I think we underestimate how much a small act of [[generosity]] can mean to someone at a low point. It also reminded me of the times people had helped me when I was new and lost. Honestly, that experience left me feeling genuinely [[fulfilled]], and it strengthened our working relationship enormously. These days he is one of the most [[dependable]] people in our office, and I like to think those evenings played a small part in that.

followUps.q: Do you often help your colleagues?
followUps.answer: Fairly often, yes. Our office is quite small, so we depend on each other a lot. If someone is stuck, it is usually quicker for everyone if we pitch in rather than let the problem grow.

followUps.q: Did he ever return the favour?
followUps.answer: He did, actually. A few months later I was buried in visa paperwork before a holiday, and he stayed late to help me finish. It felt good to know the support went both ways.

note: Set in his consultancy during application season; added the checklist detail and a closing line with 'dependable'.
